prompt: Why does a line added to a prompt's instructions cost something on every call rather than once?
hint: What is sent with each message?

choices.text: The model caches the prompt and charges again each time the cache expires
choices.why: Nothing in this lesson is cached; lesson 17 is about caches.

choices.text: The prompt is sent whole with every message
choices.why: Right: the instructions are input to every call.

choices.text: Longer prompts make the model write longer replies, and output is what costs
choices.why: Output moved by three tokens; the input moved by 97.

choices.text: Each line is checked by the harness before the call
choices.why: The harness renders the prompt; it does not check its lines.

prompt: `stats.py` reports a mean of 106.2 tokens in for `v2-json.txt` and 203.2 for `v2-long.txt`. How many extra input tokens does each call with the long prompt carry?
The total seconds were 287.4 for the short prompt and 157.0 for the long one, but the medians were 3.3 and 3.8. Which comparison should you trust, and why?
hint: What did the first run pay for that the second did not?

choices.text: The totals, because they include every call
choices.why: They include the model loading on the first run's first call, a cost of the order the runs were made in.

choices.text: The medians: one total includes loading the model
choices.why: Right: a one-off cost in one total makes the totals compare the order, not the prompts.

choices.text: Neither, because seconds are not a cost on a local model
choices.why: On your machine time is exactly what a token costs.

choices.text: The totals, because a median hides the slow calls that matter
choices.why: A median does hide the tail, but the tail here is one call loading the model.

prompt: Between the two prompts, which grew more per call: tokens in or tokens out?
hint: Compare the two means of each.

choices.text: Tokens out, because the long prompt asks for full detail
choices.why: Out grew from 30.6 to 33.6, three tokens.

choices.text: Tokens in, by 97, against 3 for tokens out
choices.why: Right: the instructions are paid as input on every call.

choices.text: Both grew by the same amount
choices.why: In grew by 97 and out by 3.

choices.text: Neither: the means are within noise of each other
choices.why: 97 tokens of input is the length of the extra instructions, the same on every call.

prompt: Line 4 of `v2-long.txt` asks for a brief summary and line 16 for full detail. Which one did `llama3.2:3b` obey?
hint: Look at `t23` and at the mean.

choices.text: Line 16, always, because it comes last
choices.why: `t23` came back shorter under the long prompt.

choices.text: Line 4, always, because it comes first
choices.why: The mean reply grew, so on some messages line 16 won.

choices.text: Neither consistently: it depends on the message
choices.why: Right: `t23` went brief, the mean went longer.

choices.text: Both: it wrote a brief summary followed by a detailed one
choices.why: Each reply had one summary of one sentence.

prompt: What happened to the summary of `t23`, the soaked parcel, under the long prompt?

choices.text: It got shorter, under the prompt that asks for detail
choices.why: Right: on that message the brief line won.

choices.text: It became the whole message, moved into the third person
choices.why: That is what the detail line asks for; it is not what came back.

choices.text: It disappeared, because the model ran out of tokens
choices.why: The reply ended on its own with all three fields.

choices.text: It was the same, word for word
choices.why: That was `t17`, almost; `t23` changed.

prompt: Why can one reply not tell you which of two conflicting instructions a model follows?

choices.text: Because replies at temperature 0 are random
choices.why: At temperature 0 they repeat on one machine.

choices.text: Which instruction wins differs from message to message
choices.why: Right: `t23` says brevity won, the mean says detail did.

choices.text: Because the model reads only the first instruction it sees
choices.why: Then line 4 would have won everywhere.

choices.text: Because a contradiction makes the model refuse
choices.why: Every reply came back.

prompt: The lesson's fix for two instructions that disagree is not a third line saying which one wins. It is to decide, and ___ the other.
You find two instructions in a prompt that disagree. What does the lesson recommend?

choices.text: Add a line saying which one wins
choices.why: That is a third instruction about the same decision.

choices.text: Put the more important one in capitals
choices.why: Capitals rank rules; they do not remove the conflict.

choices.text: Decide what you want and delete the other
choices.why: Right: one instruction per decision.

choices.text: Leave both and let the model choose per message
choices.why: That is the situation you found, and it gives you no rule.

prompt: `lint.py` prints `nothing found` for a prompt. What do you know?
hint: What is the linter made of?

choices.text: The prompt has no contradictions
choices.why: It missed *one line* against *leave nothing out*.

choices.text: That none of its patterns matched
choices.why: Right, which is weaker than saying the prompt is clear.

choices.text: The prompt will pass every check
choices.why: The linter reads the prompt, not the replies.

choices.text: The prompt is shorter than eight rules
choices.why: Length is one of several things it looks at.

prompt: Why did the linter count line 13, which opens with *Never include the customer's name*, as a line that shouts?

choices.text: Line 13 is written in capitals
choices.why: Only its first letter is.

choices.text: `where()` matches without regard to case, so *Never* counts
choices.why: Right: a finding is a line to look at, not a verdict.

choices.text: Any rule about personal data counts as shouting
choices.why: The pattern is about words, not topics.

choices.text: Line 13 repeats line 11
choices.why: That finding is about line 14.

prompt: Which of these would `lint.py` report? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: A prompt with *be brief* on one line and *in full detail* on another
choices.why: Yes: a length contradiction.

choices.text: The same instruction of four or more words written twice
choices.why: Yes: a repeated line.

choices.text: *Keep it to one line* and *leave nothing out*
choices.why: No: none of those words are on its lists.

choices.text: Two lines starting with IMPORTANT
choices.why: Yes: lines that shout.

prompt: Why is a linter that misses contradictions written in other words still worth running?
hint: What kind of mistake does it catch?

choices.text: Because it eventually learns the other words
choices.why: It is a list of patterns; it learns nothing.

choices.text: It catches mistakes that creep in unnoticed
choices.why: Right: cheap, and run before every change.

choices.text: Because it replaces the test set
choices.why: It reads the prompt; only a test set measures replies.

choices.text: Because a model reads prompts the way the linter does
choices.why: Nothing suggests that.

prompt: `pl compare --answers` printed `same answer 37, different answer 3` after the cut. What does that tell you, together with `fixed 0, broken 0`?
hint: One compares categories, the other verdicts.

choices.text: The cut changed three verdicts
choices.why: `fixed 0, broken 0`: no verdict changed.

choices.text: Three categories moved, but not one verdict changed
choices.why: Right: `t38` had no answer, `t36` and `t39` were wrong both ways.

choices.text: The long prompt was better on three messages
choices.why: Both prompts passed the same twenty-one.

choices.text: The run is not deterministic
choices.why: The two runs used different prompts; their answers may differ.

prompt: Both prompts passed 21 of 40, the same 21. What is the right reading of the cut?

choices.text: The cut made the prompt worse, because the long one parsed every reply
choices.why: Parsing more did not pass more: the same 21 pass.

choices.text: The 97 extra tokens bought nothing any check measured
choices.why: Right, and the section then asks what the checks cannot see.

choices.text: The test is too small to say anything
choices.why: It says one thing clearly: not one result moved.

choices.text: The sign test proves the prompts are equal
choices.why: p = 1.000 says there is no evidence of a difference, which is not proof of none.

prompt: Why can `cases/dev.jsonl` not tell you whether dropping the rule about customers' names was safe?
hint: Look for a name in the test set.

choices.text: Because no message in it contains a name
choices.why: Right: the count would be the same with the rule or without it.

choices.text: Because names are removed before the messages are sent
choices.why: Nothing removes them; there are none.

choices.text: Because the checks only look at `category` and `urgency`
choices.why: `summary` is not checked either, but the deeper reason is that no case could show it.

choices.text: Because a rule about names never affects a model
choices.why: It might; this test set cannot say.

prompt: How many tokens per call did cutting `v2-long.txt` down to `v2-json.txt` save, by the means `stats.py` printed?
Under the long prompt every reply parsed; under the short one `t38` did not, yet the same twenty-one passed. How can both be true?
hint: Where did `t38` fail under the long prompt?

choices.text: `t38` failed both times, at different checks
choices.why: Right: a verdict only changes when a reply crosses from fail to pass or back.

choices.text: The short prompt passed a different message to make up for it
choices.why: `fixed 0, broken 0`: no message moved either way.

choices.text: `pl check` ignores replies that do not parse
choices.why: It counts them as `json` failures.

choices.text: The long prompt's extra rules fixed the apostrophe
choices.why: Whatever it fixed, `t38` still failed a later check.

prompt: Put the steps of cutting a prompt safely in order.
items: Find the lines that make the same decision
Decide what each decision should be, and keep one line for it
Check the test set has a case for each rule you delete
Run both prompts and compare them case by case

prompt: Match each `lint.py` finding to what it means.

pairs.right: A line asking for brevity and one asking for detail
Several lines with IMPORTANT, NEVER or ALWAYS
The same instruction twice, word for word

pairs.left: rules say only what not to do
pairs.right: Three or more lines starting with *do not* or *never*

prompt: Summaries under `v2-long.txt` vary in length, and a colleague wants to add `IMPORTANT: keep the summary under 10 words` at the bottom. What do you suggest?

choices.text: Add it: the last instruction always wins
choices.why: In this lesson neither line won consistently.

choices.text: Add it in capitals, since IMPORTANT makes a model obey
choices.why: Capitals rank one rule above the others; the conflict stays.

choices.text: Replace lines 4 and 16 with one instruction
choices.why: Right: one line per decision, then measure it.

choices.text: Raise `num_predict` so the long summaries are not cut off
choices.why: No summary was cut off.
